CausalChain: Tumor cell stress → Increased production of specific tRFs → Packaging of tRFs into exosomes → Exosome secretion into the tumor microenvironment → Uptake of exosomal tRFs by immune cells → Interaction with RNA binding proteins (e.g., YBX1) → Alteration of immune cell mRNA stability and translation → Suppression of immune activation → Enhanced tumor immune evasion
Hypothesis: Exosomal tRNA-derived fragments produced by stressed tumor cells actively modulate the gene expression of immune cells by interfering with RNA binding protein-mediated mRNA regulation, thereby suppressing anti-tumor immune responses and facilitating tumor progression.
Abstract: Tumor cells under stress generate altered tRNA-derived fragments (tRFs) that are selectively packaged into exosomes and released into the tumor microenvironment. We propose that these exosomal tRFs are not merely passive biomarkers but active mediators that modulate the gene expression profile of recipient immune cells. Upon uptake by immune cells, these tRFs may interact with RNA binding proteins (such as YBX1) to alter mRNA stability and the translation of cytokines or other immune regulators, thus dampening the immune response. This exosome‐mediated communication could provide a mechanism for tumor immune evasion and progression.
